svg.text: Numbers that describe a community
The denominator decides what the number means
Three rates, three questions
Incidence: new cases in a period
is the problem still spreading
Prevalence: all existing cases at one moment
how much care must the service provide
Case fatality: deaths among those who had it
how deadly is it once you have it
A long illness has high prevalence and low incidence
Attack rate in an outbreak
Number who became ill, divided by the number
who were exposed, expressed as a percentage
Worked example
120 people ate at the funeral; 30 developed diarrhoea
30 divided by 120 equals 25 per cent
Calculate it separately for each food eaten, and the
dish with the highest rate is the likely source
Community diagnosis, in order
1. Collect data: register, survey, records, observation
2. Analyse it and rank the problems found
3. Agree priorities with the community, not for them
4. Plan with measurable objectives
5. Implement using local structures
6. Evaluate against the objectives you set
Priority weighs size, severity, community concern
and whether anything can actually be done
Why the routine data misleads
Facility records count attenders, not the population
A new clinic raises the count without raising disease
A stock-out lowers the count without lowering disease
Those who never reach a facility never appear at all
So a rise in reported cases may be a rise in reporting
Ghana reports through DHIS2 from every district
Data nobody uses at district level stops being collected
carefully. Feed the analysis back to the people who fill the forms.
